newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - HK's MTRC makes mark.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - HK's MTRC makes mark.

text.p: Hong Kong's Mass Transit Railway Corp (MTRC) launched a HK$3.5 billion revolving credit facility, its first loan issue since August 1995.
Chase Manhattan Asia, Hang Seng Finance and the Industrial Bank of Japan Hong Kong branch are joint bookrunners.

The facility will have a five-year tenor and will be available for drawings on a revolving basis during the life of the facility. The interest margin will be set at 36.5 basis points over the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR).
With fees, the all-in return to co-arrangers is 41.5 basis points, bankers said.
That's a lot less than the all-in return of around 62 basis points that the MTRC paid for a five-year average life on its previous revolver.

That amortizing deal had a final maturity of seven years with a three-year grace period. It paid a coupon of 50 basis points over HIBOR for the first three years and 56.25 basis points over HIBOR thereafter to maturity.
Forty-one banks in addition to the six arrangers joined the deal, which was raised to HK$6.0 billion.
Bankers said the current borrowing with a thinner 20 basis points margin is less attractive price-wise, but they pointed out that the MTRC is one of safest credits in Hong Kong.
Twelve banks already have joined as arrangers and underwriters.

The group includes BA Asia, Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi, Bayerische Landesbank Girozentrale Hong Kong branch, Chase Manhattan Asia, Deutsche Bank AG Hong Kong branch, Fuji Bank, Hang Seng Bank, Industrial Bank of Japan Hong Kong branch, JP Morgan Securities, Paribas Asia, Sanwa Bank Hong Kong branch and Union Bank of Switzlerand.
A mass of property-related borrowers will compete with the MTRC for Hong Kong dollars as the year comes to a close.
Among other new issues, Hong Kong's Liu Chong Hing Bank has mandated a US$80 million floating rate certificate of deposit issue.
Elsewhere, Standard and Poor's Corp announced new "public information" ratings on six Singapore, 13 Indonesian and 14 Philippines banks.
The ratings are part of S&P's new service to provide ratings unsolicited by the rated entity that are based only on publically available information.
Analysts hailed the new ratings as another source of information for international investors but cautioned that the assessments lacked the full weight of S&P's traditional ratings.
Moody's Investors Service also rates institutions that have not asked for a rating if investors demand it.
